The Tawny-throated leaftosser (Sclerurus mexicanus) is a small, insectivorous ovenbird that inhabits the forest floor of Neotropical montane regions. Field observations indicate that eggs, when incubated at an average temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], hatch after approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a developmental duration consistent with that documented in the closely related Elegant Woodcreeper (Xiphorhynchus elegans). Newly hatched nestlings emerge at a very modest initial wet weight of 2.45 grams [Ww0 = 2.45 grams], reflecting the altricial state typical of most suboscine passerines. This low natal mass imposes intense parental care demands, as brooding adults must maintain elevated body temperatures to support the chicks' rapid early development. The species' reproductive strategy is therefore tightly linked to thermal conditions in its shaded, humid understory habitat.

During the active breeding season, the basal metabolic rate of adult leaftossers has been measured under controlled laboratory conditions at a core body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], yielding a maximal resting oxygen consumption of 80 milliliters per hour [JOi = 80 milliliters per hour]. This relatively high metabolic expenditure is necessary for sustained foraging in the dim, cool microclimate of the forest floor, where arthropod prey can be scarce. Females ultimately attain a maximum adult body mass of 25.1 grams [Wwi = 25.1 grams], a significant increase from the neonatal stage that is achieved through a period of intensive provisioning by both parents. The energetic costs of reaching this mature mass are considerable, and the species' metabolic physiology appears finely tuned to the thermal stability provided by the dense canopy above.

A critical milestone in the development of young leaftossers is fledging, which, under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that characterises the active metabolic period, occurs at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching]. This relatively short nestling phase, which has also been corroborated by data from the Elegant Woodcreeper, allows the vulnerable chicks to leave the nest before they become too conspicuous to terrestrial predators. Following fledging, the juveniles remain dependent on their parents for several weeks as they learn to locate prey in the complex leaf litter. The timing of this transition is critical, as it must align with peak insect abundance to ensure the fledglings can develop their foraging skills successfully.

The onset of reproductive capacity in Sclerurus mexicanus is reached relatively quickly after independence. Puberty is attained at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at an environmental temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively early maturation suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises rapid turnover, possibly an adaptation to a high-mortality environment where the probability of surviving to a second breeding season is limited. First breeding, however, does not commence immediately upon reaching sexual maturity; instead, young birds typically wait until the following breeding season. This relatively low annual output is complemented by a recorded maximum lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] under the same thermoneutral conditions, indicating a surprisingly long-lived species for its small body size at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
